questions.q: How many different codons exist in the standard genetic code, and how many of them code for amino acids (sense codons) versus signal termination (stop codons)?
questions.a: There are 64 codons (4³). 61 are sense codons specifying amino acids; 3 (UAA, UAG, UGA) are stop codons. A wrong answer (e.g., 60 sense codons) reveals the student has not memorized the exact count or confuses start codon (AUG) as separate from sense codons — AUG codes for methionine AND signals start, so it is counted among the 61.

questions.q: The genetic code is described as "degenerate." Explain what this means and give a concrete example using the amino acid leucine.
questions.a: Degeneracy means most amino acids are specified by more than one codon. Leucine has six codons: UUA, UUG, CUU, CUC, CUA, CUG. A wrong answer that says "degenerate means the code is broken" or "each codon codes for multiple amino acids" reveals confusion between degeneracy and ambiguity — the code is degenerate but not ambiguous (each codon specifies only one amino acid).

questions.q: A tRNA molecule has the anticodon 5'-IAG-3' (where I = inosine). Using Crick's wobble rules, list all mRNA codons this tRNA can recognize and the amino acid they specify.
questions.a: Inosine at the 5' anticodon position (wobble position) pairs with U, C, or A at the 3' codon position. The anticodon 5'-IAG-3' reads codons 3'-AUC-5', 3'-AUU-5', 3'-AUA-5' (written 5'→3': CUA, UUA, AUA). These are all leucine codons (CUA, UUA) and isoleucine (AUA) — wait, AUA codes for isoleucine, not leucine. Actually, 5'-IAG-3' pairs with 3'-AUC-5' (CUA, Leu), 3'-AUU-5' (UUA, Leu), 3'-AUA-5' (AUA, Ile). But a single tRNA carries only one amino acid. This reveals the student must check: in reality, tRNA^Leu with anticodon UAG (modified to IAG) reads CUA, CUG? Let's recalc: Standard wobble: I pairs with U, C, A. Anticodon 5'-IAG-3' reads codons starting with 5'-CU? Actually, codon 5'-CUA-3' pairs with anticodon 3'-GAU-5' (written 5'-UAG-3'). If first base of anticodon is I, it's 5'-IAG-3'. It pairs with codons 5'-CUN-3' where N = U, C, A? Wait, base pairing is antiparallel. mRNA codon 5'-XYZ-3' pairs with tRNA anticodon 3'-X'Y'Z'-5'. Usually we write anticodon 5'→3'. So if anticodon is 5'-IAG-3', its 3'→5' is GAI. It pairs with codon 5'-CUN-3'? Let's do properly: Codon 5'-CUA-3' pairs with anticodon 3'-GAU-5' (5'-UAG-3'). If wobble at first position of anticodon (5' end), I can pair with U, C, A of codon third position. So anticodon 5'-IAG-3' (3'-GAI-5') pairs with codons 5'-CUU-3', 5'-CUC-3', 5'-CUA-3' (all Leu). It does NOT pair with AUA because that would require anticodon 3'-UAU-5' (5'-UAU-3'). So the correct answer: This tRNA recognizes CUU, CUC, CUA (all leucine). A wrong answer listing AUA shows misunderstanding of antiparallel pairing and wobble direction.

questions.q: Compare the genetic code properties "non-overlapping" and "comma-less." Are they synonymous? If not, give a hypothetical scenario where a code is non-overlapping but not comma-less.
questions.a: They are distinct. Non-overlapping means each nucleotide belongs to only one codon (read in triplets consecutively). Comma-less means no punctuation (spacers) between codons; the reading frame is fixed by the start codon. A hypothetical code with a "spacer" nucleotide between each triplet (e.g., AUG X UUU X UCU) would be non-overlapping (each base still used once) but NOT comma-less (it has commas/spacers). A wrong answer saying they are the same reveals the student hasn't distinguished frame maintenance from delimiter absence.

questions.q: A point mutation changes the DNA template strand sequence from 3'-TAC-5' to 3'-TAA-5' in a gene's coding region. Predict the effect on the mRNA codon and the resulting protein, assuming this is not the start codon. Justify using genetic code properties.
questions.a: Original DNA template 3'-TAC-5' → mRNA 5'-AUG-3' (Met). Mutated DNA template 3'-TAA-5' → mRNA 5'-AUU-3' (Ile). This is a missense mutation (Met → Ile). The code's degeneracy did not protect against this change because the mutation altered the second base (U→A in mRNA), which is highly specific. A wrong answer claiming "no effect because code is degenerate" shows misunderstanding that degeneracy mostly involves third-base changes, not second-base.

questions.q: Design a minimal set of tRNA anticodons (using standard bases A, U, G, C and inosine I) that can translate all six leucine codons (UUA, UUG, CUU, CUC, CUA, CUG). Explain how wobble reduces the number of tRNAs needed compared to a strict Watson-Crick pairing model.
questions.a: (1) For the UUA and UUG pair — one leucine tRNA with a modified UAA anticodon reads both codons through wobble at the third base, (2) For the CUN family — a tRNA carrying the inosine-containing IAG anticodon reads CUU, CUC and CUA, since inosine pairs with U, C or A, (3) For CUG — a separate tRNA with the CAG anticodon pairs by standard base pairing, (4) The economy — the minimal set is therefore three tRNAs instead of the six demanded by strict Watson-Crick pairing, which is exactly what the wobble hypothesis predicts. A poor answer that lists six anticodons or never uses inosine shows failure to apply the wobble rules for economy.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The genetic code is the set of rules by which ______ encoded in mRNA sequences (codons, three-nucleotide units) is translated into amino acid sequences during protein synthesis; the wobble hypothesis explains how a single tRNA anticodon can recognize multiple codons due to flexible base pairing at the third (5') position of the anticodon.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you receive a WhatsApp message written in a language where every word is exactly three letters long, there are no spaces, and the same word can mean slightly different things ______ on context — that is essentially what the ribosome reads on mRNA.

Fill in the blank: The genetic code is the set of rules by which information encoded in mRNA sequences (codons, three-nucleotide units) is translated into amino acid sequences during protein synthesis; the wobble hypothesis explains how a single tRNA anticodon can recognize multiple codons due to flexible base pairing at the third (______') position of the anticodon.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can (1) decode any given mRNA sequence into its corresponding amino acid sequence using the standard genetic code table, (2) explain the three key properties of the genetic code (universal, degenerate, non-overlapping, comma-less) with examples, and (3) apply the wobble rules to predict which codons a given tRNA anticodon can.
